query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered promising for high-heat wear-resistant use and is suitable for thin-film applications; because bulk preparation is expensive, applying it as a coating on a conventional metal is more practical. Earlier studies reported improved wear or mechanical performance from high-entropy-alloy coatings on Al, Ni, and titanium-alloy substrates, and simulations of FeNiCrCoCu on Cu indicated that sliding speed affects tangential and normal forces. Other work associated composition and grain size with changes in wear damage. However, most prior studies examined a limited operating regime or the properties of the alloys themselves rather than the overall wear resistance of coatings under varied thermal conditions. Subject to retaining FeNiCrCoCu as a coating on a Cu matrix, what single intervention could improve its overall wear resistance during sliding across varied thermal and contact regimes? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its causal mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to an unchanged coating in matched tests, the boundaries within which it should hold, supporting evidence from the introduction, and an experiment with a clear rejection criterion for both the predicted outcome and the proposed mechanism.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a nanostructured surface morphology to the FeNiCrCoCu coating on a Cu matrix will improve its overall wear resistance during sliding across varied thermal and contact regimes.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu coating on a Cu matrix
generation.mechanism: The nanostructured surface morphology will reduce the contact area between the coating and the sliding counterpart, leading to a decrease in friction and wear. This will also promote the formation of a protective tribolayer, further enhancing wear resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved wear resistance compared to an unchanged coating in matched tests
generation.baseline: Unchanged FeNiCrCoCu coating on a Cu matrix
generation.boundary: Temperature range: 20-500°C, contact pressure: 10-100 MPa, sliding speed: 0.1-10 m/s
generation.uncertainty: The actual improvement in wear resistance may vary depending on the specific nanostructured surface morphology and the testing conditions

falsification_experiment.design: Sliding wear tests with a nanostructured FeNiCrCoCu coating on a Cu matrix against a steel counterpart, with varying temperature, contact pressure, and sliding speed
measurements: Wear volume, friction coefficient, surface roughness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the wear volume of the nanostructured coating is not significantly lower than that of the unchanged coating in at least 80% of the tested conditions, the hypothesis is rejected

Cold spraying technology relative to the traditional thermal spraying technology, as well as the use of less thermal energy and more kinetic energy, greatly improves the impact speed of spraying particles on the substrate surface, and still keeps them in a solid state [,]. The results show that the impact morphology of particles is related to strain rate, in addition to material and microstructure.
